terms.gloss: a constellation, a group of stars
evidence: Cic. N. D. 1.35: signīs sīderibusque caelestibus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Properly a group of stars making a figure, as against stēlla, a single star (Macrobius, as Lewis & Short quotes him); in the poets also a single star. The Plough is Septentriōnēs, the seven stars, or Ursa Major.

terms.gloss: a constellation; a sign of the zodiac
evidence: Cic. de Or. 3.178: ad brūmāle signum
terms.comment: A figure in the sky, used above all of the twelve signs the sun passes through.
Late Latin (Ammianus, the Historia Augusta), and there a grouping of stars thought to rule a person’s fate (Lewis & Short): an astrologer’s word. Say sīdus.

phrases.latin: Vidēsne illās septem stēllās? Septentriōnēs vocantur.
phrases.english: Can you see those seven stars? They’re called the Plough.

phrases.latin: nāvita tum stēllīs numerōs et nōmina fēcit, Plēiadas, Hyadas, clāramque Lycāonis Arcton
phrases.english: then the sailor numbered the stars and named them: the Pleiades, the Hyades, and the bright Bear of Lycaon’s daughter

sources: Lewis & Short: sidus · Lewis & Short: signum · Lewis & Short: constellatio
